title: Architecture Documentation That People Actually Read
objectives: Write architecture documents that communicate clearly and drive decisions
Structure documentation around context, decisions and consequences
Apply the C4 model to create diagrams that communicate rather than confuse
Determine the minimum viable documentation for different contexts
Keep architecture documentation alive and useful over time
whyThisMatters:
Most architecture documentation goes unread. That is not an exaggeration or a joke. It is a measurable, observable reality in almost every government programme. Teams produce 60-page Solution Architecture Documents that nobody opens after the initial review meeting. They create Visio diagrams so dense with boxes and lines that they communicate nothing. They write prose so abstract it could describe any system ever built. The effort is wasted, the decisions are lost, and six months later someone asks 'why did we build it this way?' and nobody can answer.

This matters because architecture documentation is not an administrative chore. Done well, it is the primary mechanism through which architecture decisions are communicated, challenged, and preserved. It is how you ensure that the team building the system understands the design intent. It is how you enable the team that inherits the system to maintain it without reverse-engineering everything. It is how you defend your decisions when they are questioned at a spend control or service assessment.

The problem is not that architects cannot write. The problem is that most architects write for themselves rather than for their audience. They document what they find interesting rather than what their readers need to know. They aim for completeness rather than clarity. This lesson teaches you to write documentation that people actually read, because it tells them what they need to know, when they need to know it, in a format they can absorb.

content.heading: Why Most Architecture Documentation Goes Unread
content.body:
Before we talk about how to write good documentation, we need to be honest about why most of it fails.

The first reason is length. A 60-page Solution Architecture Document is not a communication tool. It is a compliance artefact. People produce it because a governance process demands it, not because anyone will read it cover to cover. The moment your document exceeds what someone can absorb in a single sitting, you have lost most of your audience.

The second reason is abstraction. Too many architecture documents read like they were written by someone who has never seen the actual system. They describe 'the integration layer' without saying what integrates with what. They reference 'the security model' without explaining what is actually protected and how. They use phrases like 'loosely coupled microservices architecture' without defining what that means in this specific context. Readers learn nothing they could not have guessed.

The third reason is timing. Documents written at the start of a project describe a system that does not yet exist. Documents written at the end describe a system that everyone already understands. The sweet spot is documentation produced during design and updated during delivery, but most teams treat documentation as a one-off activity rather than a living practice.

The fourth reason is audience confusion. A single document trying to serve the programme board, the development team, the security assessor, and the operations team will serve none of them well. Each audience needs different information at different levels of detail. When you try to satisfy everyone in one document, you satisfy no one.

The fifth reason is honesty. Many architecture documents are written to justify decisions already made rather than to communicate the reasoning honestly. They present the chosen option as obviously correct and the rejected options as obviously flawed. Readers sense this and stop trusting the document. Once trust is lost, the document becomes wallpaper.

content.heading: Writing for Your Audience
content.body:
The single most important question before you write any architecture documentation is: who will read this, and what do they need from it?

In government, your typical audiences include:

The programme board or SRO wants to understand risk, cost implications, and whether the architecture supports delivery. They do not want to know which message broker you chose. They want to know whether the system will work, what could go wrong, and what decisions need their input.

The development team wants to understand the design intent, the boundaries, the integration contracts, and the constraints they must work within. They do not want philosophy. They want enough clarity to build the right thing without having to guess what you meant.

The security assessor wants to understand the threat model, the data classification, the trust boundaries, and the security controls. They want specifics, not reassurances.

The GDS assessor wants to understand how the architecture supports the Service Standard and Technology Code of Practice. They want evidence of good decision-making, not just good technology choices.

The operations team wants to understand how to deploy, monitor, scale, and recover the system. They want runbooks and architecture that explains operational concerns, not just functional design.

The team that inherits the system in two years wants to understand why things are the way they are. They want the reasoning behind decisions, not just the decisions themselves.

Once you know your audience, you can make sensible choices about format, length, detail level, and tone. A one-page architecture brief for the programme board is a different artefact from a detailed component design for the development team. Both are valid. Neither replaces the other.

content.heading: The Minimum Viable Document
content.body:
There is a persistent myth in architecture that more documentation equals better architecture. This is wrong. More documentation usually equals more unread documentation.

The minimum viable document is the smallest artefact that achieves its communication purpose. For some contexts, that is a single page. For others, it is a detailed specification. The key is to start minimal and add detail only where it earns its place.

For a discovery or alpha phase, your minimum viable documentation might be: a context diagram showing the system boundary and external dependencies (one page), a list of key architecture decisions with brief rationale (one to two pages), a statement of constraints and assumptions (half a page), and a list of identified risks with their current status (one page).

That is four pages. It tells the team everything they need to start building. It tells the programme board everything they need to make funding decisions. It tells the assessor that you are thinking clearly.

For a beta or live phase, you will need more. But even then, the question should always be: does this section earn its place? If you remove it, would anyone notice? Would anyone make a worse decision? If the answer is no, delete it.

In government specifically, there is pressure to produce comprehensive documentation for governance and assurance purposes. Resist the temptation to pad. A concise, clear document that answers the right questions is more impressive to an assessor than a bloated document that buries the important information in noise. Assessors are experienced professionals. They can tell the difference between substance and padding.

The practical test: if you cannot explain what a section of your document is for and who will read it, that section should not exist.

content.heading: Structure That Works: Context, Decisions, Consequences
content.body:
The most effective architecture documents follow a simple structural principle: context, decisions, consequences.

Context answers: what is the situation? What problem are we solving? What constraints exist? What has already been decided? This grounds the reader in reality before you start explaining your design.

Decisions answers: what did we decide and why? What options did we consider? What trade-offs did we accept? This is the core of architecture documentation. Without clear decisions, your document is just a description of a system, not an explanation of why it is the way it is.

Consequences answers: what follows from these decisions? What risks have we accepted? What capabilities have we gained or lost? What will we need to revisit later? This helps readers understand the implications and plan accordingly.

This structure works at every level. A one-page architecture brief can follow it. A detailed design document can follow it. An Architecture Decision Record follows it. It works because it mirrors how humans actually process information: tell me where we are, tell me what we are doing, tell me what it means.

Contrast this with the typical architecture document structure: introduction, scope, assumptions, principles, logical architecture, physical architecture, security architecture, data architecture, integration architecture, deployment architecture, operational architecture, appendices. This structure is organised by topic, not by communication need. It forces the reader to hunt through multiple sections to understand a single decision. It encourages completeness over clarity.

If your organisation mandates a specific template, you can still apply the context-decisions-consequences principle within each section. The template dictates the headings; you control the content beneath them.

content.heading: Diagrams That Communicate vs Diagrams That Confuse
content.body:
Architecture diagrams are the most powerful communication tool available to you. They are also the most frequently misused.

A good diagram communicates one thing clearly. A bad diagram tries to communicate everything and communicates nothing. The difference is not artistic skill. It is clarity of purpose.

Common diagram failures in government architecture:

The 'everything diagram' that shows every system, every integration, every data flow, and every user on a single page. It looks impressive on a wall. It communicates nothing to anyone trying to understand a specific aspect of the architecture.

The 'boxes and lines' diagram where every box is labelled with a generic name ('Application Server', 'Database', 'Integration Layer') and every line is unlabelled. The reader cannot tell what the boxes actually do or what flows between them.

The 'Visio masterpiece' that uses 47 different shapes, colours, and line styles with a legend that takes up half the page. The visual complexity overwhelms the information content.

The 'aspirational diagram' that shows the target state without acknowledging the current state. It looks clean because it ignores all the messy reality that the team actually has to deal with.

Good diagrams share common traits. They have a clear title that states what the diagram shows. They have a consistent notation that the reader can learn quickly. They show only the elements relevant to the diagram's purpose. They label relationships with verbs that explain what happens between components. They include a brief key or legend if the notation is not self-evident. They state their scope explicitly, so readers know what is deliberately excluded.

The practical rule: if you cannot explain what your diagram shows in one sentence, it is trying to show too much. Split it into multiple diagrams, each with a clear purpose.

content.heading: The C4 Model in Practice
content.body:
The C4 model, created by Simon Brown, provides a structured approach to architecture diagramming that works particularly well in government contexts. It defines four levels of abstraction, each serving a different audience and purpose.

Level 1: System Context. This shows your system as a single box, surrounded by the users and other systems it interacts with. It answers the question: what is this system and how does it fit into the world? This is the diagram for your programme board, your SRO, and anyone who needs the big picture without technical detail. In government, this is where you show the relationship to GOV.UK, shared platforms, other departmental systems, and external parties.

Level 2: Container. This zooms into your system and shows the major technical building blocks: web applications, APIs, databases, message queues, file stores. It answers the question: what are the main technical components and how do they communicate? This is the diagram for your technical leadership and anyone making decisions about technology choices. In government, this is where you show which components run on which cloud platform, what sits behind the department's API gateway, and where data is stored.

Level 3: Component. This zooms into a single container and shows the major structural components within it: controllers, services, repositories, domain objects. It answers the question: how is this container organised internally? This is the diagram for your development team. Most government architecture work does not need this level of detail in formal documentation, but it is useful during design discussions.

Level 4: Code. This shows the actual code structure: classes, interfaces, relationships. In practice, this level is rarely drawn manually because it changes too frequently. Let the code be the documentation at this level.

The power of C4 is not the specific notation. It is the principle of progressive detail. You start with the big picture and zoom in only where needed. Each level serves a different audience. You never try to show everything on one diagram.

In government practice, most architecture documentation needs Level 1 and Level 2 diagrams. Level 3 is useful for complex components. Level 4 is almost never needed in formal documentation. This keeps your diagram set manageable and each diagram purposeful.

content.heading: Keeping Documentation Alive vs Letting It Rot
content.body:
The hardest problem in architecture documentation is not writing it. It is keeping it current.

Documentation rot is the natural state of architecture documents. The moment you finish writing, the system starts diverging from what you described. Requirements change. Technical decisions are revised. New integrations are added. If the documentation is not updated, it becomes actively misleading, which is worse than having no documentation at all.

There are two honest approaches to this problem.

The first approach is to keep documentation minimal and close to the code. If your architecture decisions are captured as Architecture Decision Records stored in the same repository as the code, they get updated as part of the normal development workflow. If your diagrams are generated from code or configuration (using tools like Structurizr, PlantUML, or Mermaid), they stay current automatically. This approach works well for teams with strong engineering practices.

The second approach is to accept that some documentation will become stale and design for it. Mark documents with a 'last verified' date. Include a named owner responsible for periodic review. Build documentation review into your sprint ceremonies or quarterly planning. Accept that not everything will be current all the time, but ensure the most critical documents (context diagrams, key decisions, security architecture) are reviewed regularly.

What does not work is pretending the problem does not exist. Writing a 60-page document and never updating it is worse than writing nothing, because it creates false confidence. People make decisions based on outdated information. New team members learn the wrong things.

In government, where teams change frequently and programmes run for years, documentation currency is a genuine operational risk. The practical mitigation is to keep formal documentation thin and focused on the things that change slowly (context, principles, key decisions) while accepting that detailed technical documentation lives closer to the code and is maintained by the development team.

A useful discipline: every time you make an architecture decision that changes the documented design, update the documentation in the same week. Not next sprint. Not before the next assessment. This week. If you cannot do that, your documentation is too heavy.

content.heading: When NOT to Document
content.body:
This might be the most important section in this lesson. Not everything needs architecture documentation. Knowing when not to document is as important as knowing how to document well.

Do not document decisions that are obvious or standard. If your department has a standard approach to authentication and you are using it unchanged, you do not need a page explaining why. A single sentence referencing the standard is sufficient.

Do not document things that change daily. Detailed deployment configurations, feature flags, environment-specific settings: these belong in code and configuration management, not in architecture documents. By the time you have written them down, they are wrong.

Do not document for the sake of completeness. If a section of your template adds no value for any reader, leave it out or write 'Not applicable' with a brief explanation of why. An empty section with a clear rationale is more honest than a padded section that wastes the reader's time.

Do not document what the code already says clearly. If your code is well-structured with clear naming, sensible abstractions, and good tests, it documents itself at the implementation level. Architecture documentation should explain the why and the what-at-a-high-level, not duplicate what a developer can read from the source.

Do not produce documentation that no one has asked for and no one will read. Before writing anything, ask: who needs this? When will they read it? What decision will it inform? If you cannot answer these questions, you are writing for yourself, not for your audience.

The courage to not document is underrated. In government, where there is always pressure to produce artefacts as evidence of work, it takes confidence to say 'this does not need a document, and here is why.' But the best architects produce less documentation of higher quality, and their teams thank them for it.

workedExample.title: Home Office Visa Processing Platform Documentation
workedExample.context: A Solution Architect has been asked to document the architecture for a new visa processing platform that will replace a legacy system. The platform handles sensitive personal data, integrates with multiple external systems (airlines, border systems, biometric databases), and must process 3 million applications per year. The previous architect produced a 94-page Solution Architecture Document that the development team describes as 'completely useless' and the programme board has never opened.
workedExample.approach:
The new SA takes a fundamentally different approach. Instead of rewriting the 94-page document, they start by asking: who needs what?

For the programme board, they produce a two-page Architecture Brief containing: a Level 1 context diagram showing the platform and its external dependencies, a summary of the three most significant architecture decisions with their trade-offs, the top five architecture risks with mitigations, and a one-paragraph statement of the technical approach.

For the development team, they produce a living architecture guide stored in the code repository containing: a Level 2 container diagram showing the major components and their communication patterns, a set of Architecture Decision Records (one per significant decision), interface contracts for each external integration, and a clear statement of the non-functional requirements with measurable targets.

For the security assessor, they produce a focused security architecture view containing: a data flow diagram showing where personal data moves and how it is protected, a trust boundary diagram showing where authentication and authorisation are enforced, and a mapping of security controls to identified threats.

For the operations team, they produce operational architecture documentation containing: a deployment diagram showing what runs where, a dependency map showing what fails if each component fails, and monitoring and alerting requirements.

Total documentation: approximately 20 pages across four focused artefacts, plus the ADRs in the repository. Each artefact has a named audience, a clear purpose, and a defined update trigger.
workedExample.outcome: The programme board reads and references the Architecture Brief in governance meetings. The development team uses the living guide daily and updates it as decisions change. The security assessor completes their review in half the usual time because the information they need is clearly presented. The operations team can plan their support model from the operational documentation. Six months later, when a new developer joins the team, they can understand the system's architecture within their first week by reading the repository-based documentation.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The 94-page document failed not because it lacked information, but because it tried to serve every audience in a single artefact. By splitting documentation by audience and purpose, each artefact became short enough to read, focused enough to be useful, and clear enough to maintain. The total effort to produce the new documentation set was less than maintaining the old monolithic document, because each piece was small enough to update quickly when things changed.

civilServiceScenario.title: HMRC Digital Tax Platform Documentation Overhaul
civilServiceScenario.background: HMRC's digital tax platform serves 12 million users and comprises over 200 microservices. The architecture documentation consists of a Confluence space with 847 pages, most of which were last updated between 18 months and four years ago. A recent service assessment flagged that 'the architecture documentation does not clearly communicate the current system design or the rationale for key decisions.' A new Deputy Director has asked for the documentation to be 'sorted out' before the next assessment in three months.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You cannot rewrite 847 pages of documentation in three months. You cannot verify which of the existing pages are still accurate. The development teams are focused on delivery and resistant to documentation work they see as bureaucratic overhead. The assessment panel wants evidence of clear architectural thinking, not volume.
constraints: Three months until the next service assessment
200+ microservices with varying levels of existing documentation
Development teams resistant to documentation overhead
No dedicated documentation team or technical writer
Existing Confluence space is disorganised and largely outdated
Assessment panel expects clear communication of architecture decisions
Must not disrupt ongoing delivery work
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Solution Architect responsible for the platform's architecture documentation. You have authority to set documentation standards but cannot compel development teams to do work outside their sprint commitments.
civilServiceScenario.discussion: This scenario forces you to make hard choices about what matters. You cannot fix everything. You need to identify the minimum documentation that will satisfy the assessment, serve the teams, and be maintainable going forward. Consider: What are the 10-15 most important architecture decisions that shaped this platform? Can you capture those as ADRs without needing to document every microservice? Can you produce a current Level 1 and Level 2 diagram set that shows the platform as it actually is today? Can you establish a lightweight documentation standard that teams can follow going forward without significant overhead? The temptation is to try to be comprehensive. The skill is knowing what to leave out.

practiceArtefact.description: For the HMRC scenario above, produce a documentation strategy that covers: (1) What documentation you would prioritise for the assessment, (2) What format and structure each artefact would follow, (3) How you would keep documentation current after the assessment, (4) What you would explicitly choose NOT to document and why.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Think about the assessment panel's actual needs. They want to see that you understand your system, that decisions are made deliberately, and that the architecture is communicated clearly. They do not want to read 847 Confluence pages. Your strategy should be realistic given the three-month timeline and the constraint that development teams cannot be pulled off delivery. Consider what you can produce yourself versus what needs team input. Consider what can be generated from code or infrastructure configuration versus what must be written manually.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
Documentation Strategy for HMRC Digital Tax Platform

Priority 1: Platform Context and Structure (Weeks 1-3)

Produce a single Platform Architecture Overview document (target: 8-10 pages) containing: Level 1 context diagram showing the platform, its users, and external system dependencies. Level 2 container diagram showing the major service groupings (not all 200 services individually, but the 15-20 logical groups they form). A clear statement of architecture principles governing the platform. A summary of the technology stack and hosting approach.

This can be produced by the architecture team without requiring development team input beyond validation.

Priority 2: Key Architecture Decision Records (Weeks 2-6)

Identify and document the 12-15 most significant architecture decisions as ADRs. These include: why microservices, why this hosting platform, why this integration pattern, why this authentication approach, why this data storage strategy. Write these as retrospective ADRs based on conversations with senior engineers and existing documentation fragments.

Store these in a Git repository alongside the platform's shared infrastructure code, not in Confluence.

Priority 3: Living Documentation Standard (Weeks 4-8)

Define a lightweight documentation standard for individual services: each service repository must contain a README with a one-paragraph description, a list of dependencies, and a link to any relevant ADRs. This is achievable because most teams already have partial READMEs. The standard makes expectations explicit without requiring significant new work.

Priority 4: Operational Architecture View (Weeks 6-10)

Produce a deployment and operational view showing how the platform runs in production: what infrastructure it uses, how services are deployed, how monitoring works, and what the disaster recovery approach is. Much of this can be generated from infrastructure-as-code configurations.

What We Will NOT Document: Individual service internal designs (the code is the documentation at this level). Historical decisions that no longer affect the current system. Detailed data models for each service (these live in the code). The 847 existing Confluence pages (archive them with a banner stating they are historical and may be inaccurate).

Keeping Documentation Current: ADRs are written when decisions are made, as part of the decision process. Platform overview is reviewed quarterly by the architecture team. Service READMEs are checked as part of pull request reviews. Operational views are regenerated from infrastructure code monthly.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the last architecture document you wrote. Who actually read it? How do you know? If you are not sure, what does that tell you about whether it was worth writing?

Look at your current project's architecture documentation. If a new team member joined tomorrow, could they understand the system's architecture within a week using only the existing documentation? If not, what is missing?
How much of your architecture documentation describes what the system is versus why it is that way? Which is more valuable to future readers?
When was the last time you deleted or archived architecture documentation that was no longer accurate? What stopped you from doing it sooner?
Think about a diagram you have produced recently. Could someone who was not in the room when you drew it understand what it shows without you explaining it verbally?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common reason architecture documentation goes unread?
options: Architects are poor writers
Teams are too busy to read anything
Documents are too long and not written for a specific audience
Documentation tools like Confluence are difficult to use
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The primary failure is writing documents that are too long and try to serve every audience simultaneously. When documentation is not targeted at a specific reader with specific needs, it becomes too generic and too lengthy for anyone to find value in reading it.

knowledgeCheck.question: What structural principle makes architecture documents most effective?
options: Organising by architectural layer (logical, physical, security, data)
Following the context-decisions-consequences pattern
Starting with the most technical detail and working outward
Matching the structure of the TOGAF Architecture Development Method
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The context-decisions-consequences structure mirrors how humans process information: understand the situation, understand what was decided, understand what it means. This is more effective than topic-based organisation which forces readers to hunt across sections to understand a single decision.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the C4 model, which diagram level is most appropriate for a programme board audience?
options: Level 4 (Code) showing class structures
Level 3 (Component) showing internal structure
Level 2 (Container) showing technical building blocks
Level 1 (System Context) showing the system and its external relationships
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Level 1 System Context diagrams show the system as a single box surrounded by its users and external dependencies. This gives programme boards the big picture they need without technical detail that would obscure the key messages about scope, boundaries, and dependencies.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective approach to preventing documentation rot?
options: Assigning a dedicated technical writer to maintain all documents
Scheduling annual documentation reviews
Keeping documentation minimal, close to the code, and updating it when decisions change
Using expensive enterprise documentation tools with version control
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Documentation stays current when it is minimal (less to update), stored close to the code (updated as part of normal development workflow), and updated immediately when decisions change. Annual reviews are too infrequent, and dedicated writers cannot maintain technical accuracy without architect input.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should you choose NOT to produce architecture documentation?
options: Never. All architecture decisions should be documented
When the decision is obvious, standard, or already clearly expressed in code
When the project is in discovery phase
When the team is using agile methodology
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Documentation should earn its place. Standard decisions that follow established patterns, implementation details clearly expressed in well-structured code, and information that changes too frequently to maintain in documents should not be formally documented. The skill is knowing what adds value for readers versus what adds volume without purpose.

practicalExercise.title: Documentation Rescue Mission
practicalExercise.scenario: You've joined a Home Office programme that's building a new case management system for immigration applications. The programme has been running for 8 months with three development teams. Architecture documentation consists of: a 92-page Word document written at the start of alpha (now significantly outdated), 15 Miro boards with no consistent notation, a Confluence space with 200+ pages and no clear structure, and tribal knowledge held by two senior developers who are leaving in six weeks.
practicalExercise.task:
Produce a plan to rescue this documentation situation. Specifically:

1. What would you do in the first week to stabilise the situation?
2. What core documents would you create or update, in priority order?
3. How would you capture the knowledge from the two departing developers?
4. What ongoing practices would you establish to prevent this happening again?
5. How would you get buy-in from delivery teams who see documentation as overhead?
hints: Start with what's most at risk (the departing developers' knowledge)
Don't try to update the 92-page document. Start fresh with something fit for purpose
Think about what the teams actually need day-to-day vs what governance needs occasionally
Consider pairing documentation with onboarding: if it helps new joiners, teams will value it
practicalExercise.modelAnswer:
**Week 1 Stabilisation:**
- Create a 'Documentation: Start Here' page that honestly states the current situation
- Schedule knowledge capture sessions with the two departing developers (priority: key decisions, integration patterns, known gotchas)
- Audit the Confluence space to identify the 5-10 pages that are still actively used
- Produce a fresh C4 Level 1 context diagram based on the current state

**Core Documents (Priority Order):**
1. System context diagram and narrative (what exists today, how it connects)
2. Architecture Decision Records for the 10-15 most significant decisions
3. Integration guide showing how the three teams' services connect
4. Per-service architecture README in each team's repository
5. Updated security architecture view (needed for ongoing ITHC)

**Knowledge Capture:**
- Record 30-minute sessions covering: key decisions and why, things they'd do differently, known risks and technical debt, undocumented dependencies
- Convert recordings into ADRs and architecture notes
- Have them review the new context diagram for accuracy
- Pair them with their replacements for the final two weeks

**Ongoing Practices:**
- ADRs for all significant decisions (template in each repo)
- Documentation updates as part of definition of done
- Monthly 30-minute architecture documentation review
- New joiner feedback loop: ask every new team member what was missing or confusing

**Getting Buy-in:**
- Frame documentation as onboarding investment
- Start with developer-facing docs that teams find immediately useful
- Don't mandate governance-style documents that teams see as overhead
- Show the cost of the current situation: two developers leaving with undocumented knowledge
assessmentCriteria: Prioritises knowledge at risk (departing developers) over comprehensive documentation
Starts with what's useful to teams, not what governance demands
Establishes sustainable practices rather than one-off documentation efforts
Recognises that the 92-page document should be replaced, not updated

commonMistakes: Writing a 60-page SAD that nobody reads because it tries to document everything at the same level of detail
Drawing diagrams without labels, keys, or context that become meaningless within weeks
Treating documentation as a phase that happens before development rather than a continuous practice
Using inconsistent notation across diagrams so readers can't build a mental model
Storing documentation in locations that teams can't find or don't know about
Perfecting documentation instead of shipping it in useful-but-imperfect form
Writing for auditors and governance rather than for the people who actually need to understand the architecture
Failing to archive outdated documentation, leaving readers unsure what's current

weakVsStrong.weak: A weak SA produces a 75-page Solution Architecture Document using the departmental template, filling in every section including those that aren't relevant. The document takes three weeks to write, is reviewed once, approved, and filed in SharePoint. Six months later, the architecture has changed significantly but the document hasn't been updated. New team members are pointed to it but find it confusing because it describes a system that no longer exists. The SA considers documentation 'done' and moves on to other work.
weakVsStrong.strong: A strong SA produces a 12-page living architecture document in Markdown, stored in the team's Git repository. It has a clear context diagram, a container diagram, a section on key decisions (linking to ADRs), and a section on cross-cutting concerns. It's reviewed in pull requests whenever the architecture changes. New team members can understand the system within a day of reading it. The programme board gets a one-page summary extracted from it quarterly. The SA treats documentation as a product that serves its users, iterating based on feedback.

workplaceSignals: New team members can understand your architecture within their first week by reading your documentation
Your diagrams are referenced in team discussions and decision-making, not just filed away
Programme boards can explain the architecture at a high level because your summaries are clear
When architecture decisions are questioned, you can point to documented rationale rather than relying on memory
Your documentation has been updated within the last month and reflects the current state of the system
Other teams ask to use your documentation approach or templates as a model
GDS assessors comment positively on the clarity of your architecture documentation
You spend more time maintaining documentation incrementally than writing large documents from scratch
